scenes.script_line: This is where the real work begins. In step four, you'll unpack the old story you've been telling yourself, in as much detail as you can. Why go into it so fully? Because you can't change what you can't see. Most old stories live in the background, as a vague feeling or a familiar voice. While they stay vague, they stay powerful. When you write them down, in detail, you bring them into the light. And what's in the light can be questioned.

scenes.script_line: Before you begin, it helps to understand one distinction. There's what happened, and there's what you made it mean. What happened might be: "I was passed over for a promotion." What you made it mean might be: "I'll never be good enough." The event is a fact. The meaning is the story. In this step, you're writing the meaning in all its detail.

scenes.script_line: And pay attention to the voices. Often, the harshest lines in our stories aren't even ours. They're things we heard from a parent, a teacher, a boss, or a friend, and quietly started repeating to ourselves. Write them down exactly as you hear them. Page nine gives you six tips for writing your old story. Let loose. Write freely, and let go of grammar and neatness. Amplify. Turn up the tones, emotions and voices that make up the story. Colour. Bring in as much depth and detail as you can, and let yourself feel it. Voices. Capture the voices inside the story, whether they're yours, your parents'

scenes.script_line: As you write, you'll start to notice limiting beliefs. A limiting belief is simply a belief about the way something is, that holds you back from moving toward your goals. Limiting beliefs are built from evidence that seems real. But when that evidence is questioned, it often turns out to be false. To help you dig deeper, ask yourself these questions. Who, what and how might be behind this story? If you feel defensive about it, what are you actually defending? What fears, and what ultimate fear, has this story been protecting? scenes.script_line: If you're struggling to start, try beginning with this sentence: "The story I've been telling myself is…" Then just keep writing, without stopping to judge or correct. Here's part of Sam's old story. "I'm not good enough to lead. Leaders are confident, and I'm not. My dad always said, don't get too big for your boots. Whenever I speak up, I worry I'll say something stupid, so it's safer to stay quiet. If I went for the role and failed, everyone would see I was a fraud." Can you see the beliefs woven through it? scenes.script_line: This step can stir things up, and that's okay. It's a sign you're getting close to what matters. If it gets heavy, pause. Breathe. Step away for a moment if you need to. Your facilitator is in the room for exactly this reason, so let them know if you'd like support. You can write several drafts. In fact, many people do. When you're ready, write your final version on page ten, with extra space on page eleven. Be as specific as you can, and unearth as many layers as possible. Your facilitator is here to support you. Take your time.
